Suncor, Cenovus ride refining boom to record-setting results 

Both Cenovus and Suncor own refineries in Canada and the U.S., which cushioned the businesses when prices for heavy Canadian oil faltered

By
James Rose
November 4, 2026 at 2:17 p.m.
Last Updated: November 4, 2026 at 2:40 p.m.

Two of Canada’s biggest oil producers posted record results this week, with Suncor Energy Inc. generating more cash than ever before and Cenovus Energy Inc. pumping more than a million barrels a day for the first time in its history.

Both Calgary-based companies leaned on their refineries for a boost, and both are handing more of the windfall back to shareholders.

“We’re in a global commodity business that is cyclical in nature,” said Suncor chief executive Rich Kruger in a Wednesday morning conference call. “We have to just have an endless, ruthless, unwavering commitment to cost management.”

Cenovus chief executive Jon McKenzie struck a similar note on his own call.

“This is a commodity business, and the low-cost producer wins, and across our oilsands base, not only (are we) the biggest producer, but we are the lowest-cost producer as well,” he said.

Two years ago, Suncor was dealing with a string of workplace accidents, sputtering operations and an activist investor at the door.

On Tuesday, the company said it brought in $6.7 billion in adjusted funds from operations — a measure of the cash it generates — in the three months ended Sept. 30, its best quarter ever and up 75 per cent from a year earlier.

Profit for the producer, which also owns the Petro-Canada chain of gas stations, more than doubled to $3.8 billion.

“Wow, what a quarter for me to begin my role as CFO,” said Peter Zeuty, Suncor’s new chief financial officer.

Suncor raised its quarterly dividend by 10 per cent and boosted its monthly share buybacks to $750 million from $500 million. It now expects to repurchase $5.5 billion of its own stock this year.

“Every member of our board and our executive team treats our dividend as an unbreakable promise to our shareholders,” Zeuty added.

Kruger, who plans to step down next spring, framed the quarter around three goals: finishing the year’s major maintenance, setting up a strong close and maximizing value in a high-price market. “All three were met,” he said.

During a 37-day maintenance project at its Edmonton refinery this fall, one employee had an idea to avoid a shutdown and keep the facility running. The novel workaround preserved roughly 46,000 barrels a day of throughput and adding more than $50 million to free cash flow, Kruger told analysts.

“$50 million. One idea by one person,” Kruger said. “This idea wasn’t in our annual business plan, and it wasn’t in our March investor deck.”

Suncor controls nearly every step of its oil’s journey from the ground to the gas tank, including mining bitumen from the oilsands, upgrading and refining it, and selling the fuel at its own stations. It sold a third-quarter record of roughly 677,000 barrels a day of gasoline, diesel and other fuels at home and abroad.

“Suncor handily beat consensus expectations thanks to exceptionally strong downstream performance,” said analyst Randy Ollenberger of BMO Capital Markets in a note to investors.

Oilsands production dipped slightly from a year earlier, largely because of maintenance at Syncrude, the mine north of Fort McMurray in which Suncor holds a majority stake. Overall upstream production still came in at a sturdy 853,000 barrels a day.

Suncor also confirmed it is leaving the offshore business off Newfoundland and Labrador.

In early October, it agreed to sell its stakes in the Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose projects to U.K. North Sea producer Ithaca Energy PLC for $1.2 billion, plus as much as $350 million more if oil prices hold up.

The sale fits Kruger’s focus on the Alberta oilsands, where Suncor has decades’ worth of reserves.

The company booked $3.5 billion in income taxes and royalties in the quarter, mostly payable in Canada, bringing its nine-month total to $8.1 billion.

Kruger made a point of it, saying the company is “returning tremendous value to Canadians with significantly higher royalty payments and income taxes.”

Suncor left its full-year production and spending forecasts unchanged.

Cenovus, meanwhile, joined a small club of Canadian producers operating at the million-barrel scale.

Its output averaged just over one million barrels of oil equivalent per day in the third quarter, up more than 50,000 barrels a day from the spring. Cenovus is the country’s second-biggest oil producer behind Canadian Natural Resources Ltd., with Suncor third.

The milestone caps a period of rapid expansion for Cenovus, which bought Husky Energy in 2021 and MEG Energy Corp. in 2025, and announced last month it will buy smaller oilsands rival Athabasca Oil Corp.

Cenovus earned $3.4 billion in the quarter, up from $2.9 billion in the three months before.

Most of the gain came from the oilsands, where its Foster Creek, Christina Lake and Sunrise projects each set production records, for a combined fresh high of 833,000 barrels a day.

Like Suncor, Cenovus owns refineries in Canada and the United States, which cushioned the business when prices for heavy Canadian oil faltered.

While its oil-producing business earned a little less, refining profits nearly doubled from the spring.

Cenovus handed $1.9 billion back to investors, mostly through share buybacks, and cut its net debt by $2.4 billion to $3 billion.

The Athabasca deal, valued at about $5.7 billion including debt, would add roughly 45,000 barrels a day of production. It needs approval from Athabasca shareholders and an Alberta court. It’s expected to close in December.

In August, Cenovus sold its Canadian commercial fuels business to BVD Petroleum Inc. for about $260 million.

Cenovus shares fell roughly five per cent in Toronto Wednesday morning to around $41, despite the earnings beat. The stock is still up roughly 80 per cent since January.
